items.title: The Field of a Charged Conducting Sphere

source_refs.note: The Field of a Charged Conducting Sphere: a main subheading of 9.4 Gauss's law, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 200-201.

blocks.text: Consider a conducting sphere of radius R containing a charge q. We know that all the charge is distributed uniformly over the surface of sphere as shown in Fig. 9.15. We can also conclude from the spherical symmetry that the electric field is radial everywhere and that its magnitude depends only on the distance r from the centre of the sphere. Thus, the magnitude E is uniform over a spherical surface with any radius r concentric with the spherical conductor. Therefore, we take our Gaussian surface as an imaginary sphere with radius r greater than the radius R of the conducting sphere.
The area of the Gaussian sphere is 4πr², and because E is uniform over the sphere, the total flux through the whole surface will be:

blocks.alt: An inner circle (the conducting sphere, radius R, marked in cyan) with + charges on its surface, and a larger concentric circle (the Gaussian sphere, radius r). Magenta field lines run radially outward beyond both circles, dashed inside the conductor.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.15 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.15).

blocks.text: This shows that the field at any point outside the sphere is the same as though the entire charge were concentrated at its centre. Just outside of the sphere, where r = R, i.e.,

blocks.latex: \text{In vector form:} \qquad \vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{q}{R^2}\,\hat{r} \qquad \text{where } \hat{r} \text{ is the direction of } \vec{E}.
blocks.text_alt: In vector form:   E = (1/4πε₀)(q/R²) r̂   where r̂ is the direction of E.
